terminal, and no other file, is read. If that file is missing or empty when you
stop, the task scores zero however good your analysis was.

You are working against a time limit and will be cut off without warning when it

you refinement rather than the whole attempt. Answer in prose, and state each

# Escalator orientation in the department store video

## Answer

**The escalator that goes up to the next floor is oriented left to right: its bottom landing is on the left and its top is on the right.** A shopper boarding it at the bottom would be carried upward and to the right as seen from this viewpoint. It is *not* oriented right to left.

## What the scene contains

The clip is a slow rightward pan across a department-store men's shoe department — mirrored columns, shoe display tables, a striped-shirt shopper, and two mannequins standing among birch-log poles. Behind and above the mannequins is the store's escalator well, which stays in frame for essentially the whole 14.5 seconds.

Inside that well there are **two escalator flights that cross each other in an "X"** (a criss-cross / scissor pair). Both of them connect the floor the camera is standing on with the floor above; one carries people up and the other carries them down. They are offset in depth, so they cross visually without touching.

- **Flight A (the near one, the prominent one with the thick green-tinted glass balustrade):** it runs from **lower-left to upper-right**. Its two dark handrails and the glass panel descend toward the left and pass behind a white column just above floor level, and the white triangular soffit (the underside cladding of the escalator truss) slopes down toward the left as well, so its bottom landing is on the left on this floor. Its upper end climbs to the right and passes up through the ceiling opening onto the floor above.
- **Flight B (the farther one):** it runs the opposite way, from **lower-right to upper-left**. Its handrails pass behind flight A's glass balustrade where the two cross, and its bottom landing is down and to the right, tucked behind one of the marble-based columns.

## How I determined which flight is the "up" one

Because the two flights cross, identifying the slope alone is not enough — one of them is the down escalator. I settled it by tracking a rider.

I extracted the video at 10 fps, measured the camera motion (it is an almost purely horizontal pan — about 589 px of scene shift to the left over 14 s, with essentially zero vertical drift), and then tracked a dark-clothed figure in camera-motion-compensated "scene" coordinates over the first ~4 seconds. The figure's centroid moved perfectly smoothly and at constant velocity from (838, 64) to (904, 90) — i.e. about **+17 px/s to the right and +7 px/s downward**, a trajectory slope of about **+0.39 (going down as it goes right)**. That constant-velocity, no-gait-wobble motion is the signature of someone standing on a moving escalator, and the trajectory slope matches the measured slope of flight B (about +0.44, measured from its handrails) rather than flight A, whose slope is negative (it rises to the right).

So the person was **riding flight B downward**, which makes flight B the down escalator. That leaves **flight A — the near, glass-balustraded flight that rises from lower-left to upper-right — as the escalator going up to the next floor.** This is also consistent with the people seen gathered at the bottom of flight B on the right-hand side later in the clip, where riders step off the down escalator.

## Conclusion

From this viewpoint in the department store, the escalator going up to the next floor runs **from left to right, bottom to top**: you step on at the lower left and it carries you up toward the upper right, through the ceiling opening to the floor above. The crossing flight beside it, which runs right-to-left from bottom to top, is the down escalator.

# Escalator orientation

## Answer

From this viewpoint in the department store, the escalator going up to the next floor is oriented **left to right from the bottom to the top**.

That is: the bottom landing is on the left side of the view and the top landing is on the right side of the view. A shopper riding up travels toward the right of the frame as they ascend.

## How this was determined

- The video (14.5 s, 854x480) was sampled at 1, 2, and 5 frames per second, and the escalator region was cropped and enlarged.
- The left portion of the early frames is a tall mirror reflecting the shoe department; the real escalator is the direct view on the right side of the frame, so the mirror image was excluded from the orientation judgment.
- The real escalator structure is a solid white side wall beneath glass balustrades with black handrails. Its low end (short wall, near the mannequin display and pillars) is on the left, and it rises to meet the upper-floor ceiling opening on the right. Tracing the handrail in a mid-video frame, the incline runs from about lower-left to upper-right: as image x increases, the rail height increases (image y decreases).
- Around 1–5 s, a rider is visible at the upper-right landing who then rides down and to the left along the incline, reaching mid-span a few seconds later. This confirms the incline axis runs lower-left to upper-right: the down lane descends from upper-right to lower-left.
- The up lane serving the same two floors is the parallel twin in the same well, so it shares that same incline axis: its bottom is likewise on the left and its top on the right. Hence going up means going from left to right.
- The oppositely sloped glass seen crossing above/behind (forming an X in zoomed views near 12–13 s) is the next flight up (second floor to the floor above), arranged as a switchback rising from right to left. It is not the ground-to-next-floor flight the question asks about.
